title: Jamaica After Hurricane Melissa: The IMF's Verdict on the Recovery | Across the Water, Ep. 11
lede: Hurricane Melissa caused US$8.8 billion in physical damage to Jamaica, about 41% of 2024 GDP, by the World Bank and IDB's estimate. A year on, the IMF says the economy contracted 1.2% in fiscal 2025/26, far less than the 4.3% it projected in January. This episode explains how insurance, emergency loans and a record month of diaspora remittances carried the recovery, and why inflation is now the squeeze.
keyPoints: Physical damage US$8.8 billion, about 41% of Jamaica's 2024 GDP (World Bank and IDB, Nov 2025).
Early money about US$662 million, including a US$150 million catastrophe bond paid in full and US$91 million from CCRIF; lenders assembled up to US$6.7 billion over three years (IMF).
The IMF says the economy contracted 1.2% in FY2025/26 and projects 1.3% growth in FY2026/27, with pre-storm output by mid-2027 (IMF Article IV statement, Nov 11, 2026).
Remittances reached US$3.12 billion in FY2025/26, up 6.7%, with a record US$296 million in December 2025 (Bank of Jamaica data).
Inflation hit 8.6% in September 2026, above the 4–6% target; the Bank of Jamaica raised its policy rate to 6% (STATIN; Bank of Jamaica).
